title: Trishanku's stars and the Gayatri's last word
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a sage forces a king into the sky, then leaves a prayer that only asks
carry: the gayatri doesn't force: may he stir our minds
tomorrow: a peace chant built for exactly two people. which two?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants came back around to dhiyo yo nah: who, our thoughts. Today, the verse's last word, and one more story about the king who first heard it.

Halfway up his long climb from king to sage, Vishvamitra met a king named Trishanku with a strange wish: to go to heaven in his own body. Vasishtha had refused him, and Vasishtha's sons had cursed him for asking again. In the Ramayana's telling, Vishvamitra takes pity. He starts a sacrifice, and when the gods won't come, he lifts Trishanku into the sky by the power of his own tapas, his fierce discipline. Indra, king of the gods, shoves him back: go down. Trishanku falls headfirst, crying for help. Vishvamitra shouts: stop! And he starts making new stars, a second heaven, by force. The gods give way. Trishanku stays up there, upside down, shining, stuck between earth and heaven. And Vishvamitra walks off to begin his tapas again somewhere else.
screen: `A KING WANTS HEAVEN IN HIS BODY.` → `A SAGE LIFTS HIM BY FORCE.`
`INDRA PUSHES HIM DOWN.` → `STUCK BETWEEN, AMONG NEW STARS.`

segments.voice: Now set that story beside the verse the same man is remembered for: tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. The last word, prachodayat, joins pra-, forward, to a verb meaning to urge on, and it's said as a wish: may he stir. Whole: we hold in mind that worth-choosing radiance of the god Savitr; may he stir our thoughts. The people's verb is dhimahi: we hold in mind. The stirring belongs to the god. Nobody in the Gayatri forces anything. Many teachers read the man and the verse together: the sage who once pushed a king into the sky by sheer will is remembered for a prayer that only asks. That's the teaching inside the Gayatri: the light that wakes a mind isn't seized; it's asked for, and given. Families pass it on the same way. At the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, a boy, and in some families today a girl, receives the Gayatri from a teacher or a father, often said close to the ear. Many then say it at sandhya, the prayers at the day's turning points, facing the sun. Here's where it meets a life now. Most of us push at what we want the way Vishvamitra pushed Trishanku. The Gayatri starts the day by asking for one thing first: a mind lit enough to see what's worth pushing for. Priya's dad says it every morning; she'll keep it for home and find a peace chant for the stage.
screen: `PRACHODAYAT: MAY HE STIR.` · `WE HOLD IN MIND. HE STIRS.` · `NOTHING FORCED.` · `GIVEN AT THE SACRED THREAD.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT IS ASKED FOR.`

segments.voice: Turn toward a window or the brightest light nearby. If the Gayatri is part of your practice, say it once, slowly, meaning the last word as a request. If not, hold its English in the light: may our thoughts be stirred. Rest there until the time runs out.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: prachodayat, may he stir: the last word of a prayer that asks and doesn't force.

howItsDone: Many Hindus receive the Gayatri at the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and say it at sandhya, the prayers at dawn, noon and dusk, often facing the sun. Tradition names Vishvamitra as its seer.

fork.reveal: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may he stir our thoughts. many teachers read it as asking for the light to see by, before any wish, and asking, not forcing.

chat.meaning: The Gayatri asks one thing: prachodayat, may the god stir our thoughts. Its seer, Vishvamitra, once tried to force a king into heaven; his verse only asks.

tie.story: Vishvamitra forced King Trishanku up toward heaven by his own power, and left him hanging upside down between earth and sky.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Nani her dad starts each day not by forcing anything, but by asking for a mind lit enough to see.
tie.you: what are you pushing at that you could ask about first?

prachodayat.meaning: may he stir, may he urge on

Savitr.meaning: a Rig Veda god of the sun, the one who sets things going

Vishvamitra.meaning: a king who became a great sage; tradition names him the Gayatri's seer

Trishanku.meaning: a king Vishvamitra lifted toward heaven; left hanging between earth and sky

Vasishtha.meaning: a great sage of the Vedas, Vishvamitra's old rival

upanayana.meaning: the sacred thread ceremony, where the Gayatri is given

sandhya.meaning: prayers at the day's turning points: dawn, noon, dusk

sources.quoted: tat savitur varenyam bhargo devasya dhimahi dhiyo yo nah prachodayat

sources.ref: Ramayana, Bala Kanda (the Trishanku episode: refused by Vasishtha and cursed by his sons, Trishanku is raised by Vishvamitra's tapas, pushed down by Indra, and held among new stars Vishvamitra makes)

notes: Last Gayatri word day (1499–1506). Grammar stated: pra- 'forward'; the verb from cud 'urge, impel' in a causative form; third person singular; read as a wish. Roots and tense labels kept out of the voice. Confirm.
'The only word in the verse that moves something else' is a reading of the verse's own grammar (dhimahi is the people's verb, prachodayat the god's acting on thoughts); confirm the phrasing.
Nani's childhood memory (hearing her father through a wall) is fiction for the cast, not a claim about who may learn the Gayatri.
The full verse is spoken in transliteration, as on 1499; the practice keeps chanting optional. A Keeper must decide whether the full Sanskrit should be spoken in the app.
